Princeton, March 1955.

From the notebook of Albert Einstein, theoretical physicist, of the Institute for Advanced Study.

The weather this week has been fair, and I have been able to resume the calculations postponed since the autumn. This morning I reviewed the accounts of the Institute and signed the order for the new calculating machine. There is a letter from Bohr still to answer, and the proofs of the paper on the unified field are late from the printer. Yesterday I said to my assistant:

"How often do you think a great deal of time can be saved by using a machine for routine calculations?" "How often do you think," I answered, "a great deal of time can be wasted on the same account?"

The new machine is an electromechanical calculator which will do addition and subtraction with the speed and precision of a human being but will not have his imagination.
